about: The academic writing framework behind the Write screen. Stages and checks follow the University of Melbourne Academic Skills 'Academic Writing' series (paraphrased, not quoted); structures it does not cover come from IMRaD, Swales' CARS model, the Manchester Academic Phrasebank's moves and the citation style manuals. docs/academic-writing.md.

videos.1n15ZkcX5sM: Structure and key elements of academic paragraphs

video_source: Academic Skills, The University of Melbourne (YouTube)

stages.title: Analyse the task
stages.why: Most marks are lost by answering a different question from the one set. Read the brief and the marking rubric together before anything else.
stages.produce: A task card: what kind of writing it is, what it must do, for whom, the word limit and the sections it needs.
checklist: Find the direction word (discuss, evaluate, compare, argue…) and write what it asks you to do
Underline the content words: the topic itself
Note the limiting words: the place, time, group or number of sources that narrow it
List the sections or parts the task requires
Set the word limit, and aim to land within 10% of it
Read the marking rubric beside the brief

stages.title: Choose your focus
stages.why: A clear focus or research question decides what you read, what you keep and what you leave out.
stages.produce: For research work: a research question and a one-sentence purpose statement. For reflection: one theme.
checklist: Brainstorm everything you know and want to find out
Narrow to one focus that the word limit can carry
For research: phrase it as a question that starts with what, how, why or to what extent
It cannot be answered with yes, no or a single number
It names its scope: who, where, when
You can say in one sentence why it matters (the 'so what?')

stages.title: Read and take notes
stages.why: Reading with your plan in mind turns notes into the first draft of your evidence.
stages.produce: A source list, each judged for quality, and notes in your own words with the author, year and page.
checklist: Prefer peer-reviewed and authoritative sources; note bias and currency
Write notes in your own words, with author, year and page
Mark any exact wording as a quote
Add your own response to each note: agree, doubt, connects to…
Tag each note with the part of your plan it supports

stages.title: Plan the argument
stages.why: A plan with a thesis and a word budget keeps every paragraph working for the answer.
stages.produce: Your thesis (the position you take), the sections in order, a topic sentence for each paragraph and a word budget.
checklist: Write your thesis in one or two sentences
Put the sections in the order your thesis previews them
Give each section at least one piece of evidence
For argument: include the strongest counter-argument and your reply
Budget the words: about 5% introduction, 90% body, 5% conclusion
For a literature review: choose thematic, chronological, by perspective or by method

stages.title: Draft the body
stages.why: Each paragraph makes one point, backs it with evidence and says what that evidence means.
stages.produce: Body paragraphs: topic sentence, evidence, interpretation, link back to the thesis.
checklist: Open each paragraph with a topic sentence stating its one idea
Support it with evidence, mostly paraphrased and cited
Explain what the evidence shows and why it matters
Start and end paragraphs in your own voice, not a source's
In reviews: describe, then critique, then suggest, then credit strengths
In reflection: describe briefly, then interpret, evaluate and plan

stages.title: Connect and sharpen your voice
stages.why: Readers follow an argument through its links: between sentences, between paragraphs, and back to the thesis.
stages.produce: A draft whose ideas flow, with your critical position visible throughout.
checklist: Choose linking words that match the real relation: addition, contrast, cause, condition
Start sentences with what the reader knows and end with what is new
Keep key terms consistent; define abbreviations on first use
Connect sources to each other: agree, disagree, build on
Use reporting verbs that show your stance (suggests, argues, overlooks)

stages.title: Write the introduction and conclusion
stages.why: Written last, they can promise exactly what the body delivers.
stages.produce: An introduction that moves from context to focus to thesis to structure, and a conclusion that concludes.
checklist: Introduction: context, then your focus, then your thesis, then how the piece is organised
Avoid sweeping openers ('since the beginning of time')
Conclusion: restate the thesis, sum up the main points, say what they show
Add no new evidence or citations in the conclusion
Each takes about 5% of the words

stages.title: Revise for style and clarity
stages.why: Academic style is precise, formal and measured: claims as strong as the evidence, no stronger.
stages.produce: A second and third draft, edited for clarity and tone.
checklist: Aim for sentences of about 15 to 25 words; split very long ones
No contractions (don't, it's) or vague words (thing, a lot, good)
Use 'I' only where the genre allows it, such as reflection
Hedge claims to match the evidence (suggests, may, is likely)
Put the important information at the end of the sentence

stages.title: Paraphrase and cite
stages.why: Every idea that is not yours is credited, and in your own words wherever possible.
stages.produce: Consistent in-text citations and a complete reference list in the required style.
checklist: Paraphrase: read, set the source aside, write from memory, then compare
Keep direct quotes under 10% of the text, each with a page number
Mix author-first ('Smith (2020) shows…') and idea-first ('… (Smith, 2020)') citations
Every in-text citation has an entry in the reference list, and the other way round
Use the one style the task requires, consistently

stages.title: Check and proofread
stages.why: The last pass catches what costs easy marks.
stages.produce: A final draft checked against the brief and the rubric.
checklist: Within 10% of the word limit
Every key term from the brief appears
Every required section is there
Spelling, grammar and punctuation read aloud or checked
Formatting and reference list follow the required style

genres.title: Essay
genres.summary: An argument that answers a question, in continuous prose with no headings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.hint: Context, then your focus, then your thesis, then how the essay is organised.

sections.title: First main point
sections.hint: Topic sentence, evidence, what it shows, link back to the thesis.

sections.title: Second main point
sections.hint: In the order your thesis previews. One idea per paragraph.

sections.title: Third main point or counter-argument
sections.hint: Address the strongest objection and answer it.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.hint: Restate the thesis, sum up, say what it all shows. No new evidence.

genres.title: Literature review
genres.summary: A critical synthesis of what is known, organised to show where the gap is.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.hint: The topic, why it matters, the scope (which literature, which years) and how the review is organised.

sections.title: Theme 1
sections.hint: Group sources by theme, not one by one. Describe, critique, and say what they mean together.

sections.title: Theme 2
sections.hint: Show where sources agree, disagree and build on each other.

sections.title: Theme 3
sections.hint: Judge the methods, samples and applicability, not only the findings.

sections.title: Gaps and directions
sections.hint: What the literature does not yet answer: this is where your research question comes from.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.hint: What is known, what is not, and why the gap matters.

genres.title: Research paper
genres.summary: An empirical study in the IMRaD structure: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.hint: In 150 to 250 words: background, aim, method, main result, conclusion. Written last.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.hint: Swales' CARS moves: establish the territory, show the gap, then say how this study fills it.

sections.title: Methods
sections.hint: Enough detail to repeat the study: participants, materials, procedure, analysis. Past tense.

sections.title: Results
sections.hint: What you found, with statistics, tables and figures. Report, do not interpret.

sections.title: Discussion
sections.hint: What the results mean, how they compare with the literature, limitations and implications.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.hint: The answer to the research question and what should happen next.

genres.title: Research proposal
genres.summary: A plan for a study: what you will ask, why it matters, and how you will answer it.

sections.title: Summary
sections.hint: The question, why it matters, the method and the expected contribution in one paragraph.

sections.title: Background and rationale
sections.hint: What is known, the gap, and why filling it matters now.

sections.title: Research question and aims
sections.hint: The question, a purpose statement, and two to four objectives.

sections.title: Literature review
sections.hint: The studies your question builds on, critically, grouped by theme.

sections.title: Methodology
sections.hint: Design, participants or data, instruments, analysis, and why they suit the question.

sections.title: Ethics
sections.hint: Consent, risk, data protection and approvals needed.

sections.title: Timeline
sections.hint: The main stages and when each will be done.

sections.title: Expected outcomes and significance
sections.hint: What you expect to find and who it will help.

genres.title: Reflective writing
genres.summary: Learning from an experience, in the first person, linked to theory.

sections.title: Describe
sections.hint: Briefly, what happened. Keep this the smallest part.

sections.title: Interpret
sections.hint: What it meant, how you felt, and why, linked to your readings.

sections.title: Evaluate
sections.hint: What went well or badly and what you learned. Be honest and specific.

sections.title: Plan
sections.hint: What you will do differently next time, and how.

genres.title: Report
genres.summary: Findings and recommendations for a reader who needs to act, organised under headings.

sections.title: Executive summary
sections.hint: Purpose, key findings and recommendations, readable on its own.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.hint: Purpose, scope and background.

sections.title: Findings
sections.hint: What you found, under clear numbered headings, with evidence.

sections.title: Discussion
sections.hint: What the findings mean for the reader.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.hint: Specific, actionable steps, each tied to a finding.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.hint: The main message in a few sentences.
